claims.text: As-deposited nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi films or nanoribbons possess chemical inhomogeneity and residual stress.
Nanoscale chemical heterogeneities and interface regions act as domain-wall pinning sites in FeMnNiGeSi films or nanoribbons.
Chemical disorder and residual stress produce nonuniform magnetic exchange interactions.
Chemical disorder and residual stress enhance domain-wall pinning.
Nanoscale chemical inhomogeneity and residual stress largely govern the low-field magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of the proposed FeMnNiGeSi structures.
These microstructural features reduce the maximum magnetic entropy change relative to analogous bulk samples.
Domain-wall pinning causes sluggish wall motion and additional magnetic hysteresis.
Hysteretic losses can be important in magnetocaloric refrigeration systems.
Limited heat transfer at small dimensions produces thermal lag and constrains cycle frequency.
A mild inert-atmosphere anneal at approximately 250 degrees Celsius will partially relax residual stress.
The mild anneal will make the nanoscale chemical distribution more homogeneous while preserving the nanostructure.
Reducing stress and chemical clustering will make low-field domain motion more reversible.
Annealing will mitigate thermal lag caused by constrained heat transfer.
Relative to the as-deposited control, annealed samples will exhibit a higher maximum magnetic entropy change under identical low-field cycling.
Relative to the as-deposited control, annealed samples will exhibit narrower hysteresis loops and lower coercivity.
Annealed samples will tolerate higher cycle frequencies without magnetocaloric performance degradation.
The proposed intervention applies at fields below 0.5 T and within the magnetic-transition temperature range.
Excessive annealing temperature or duration may cause grain growth or phase separation.
